newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Foreign experts cautions on Bosnia bank agreement.
newsitem.headline: Foreign experts cautions on Bosnia bank agreement.

text.p: An agreement among Bosnian leaders on a single central bank and currency is a step forward but many significant issues remain to be resolved, foreign analysts said on Wednesday.
"It's like always in Bosnia, the devil is in the detail," a foreign economic expert told Reuters.

After months of negotiations, Bosnia's Serb, Moslem and Croat presidency members on Tuesday agreed to the principle of a single central bank and a single currency, accepting the concept set out in a peace treaty they signed in 1995.

The presidency also announced the name of the country's future single currency -- "convertible mark" -- and agreed on an interim bank note called a "convertible coupon" to last until the permanent currency is in place.

In a compromise deal, Serbs dropped their demands for separate central banks but won a concession which allows different design features in Bosnia's two territories -- the Moslem-Croat federation and the Serb republic.

Western officials familiar with the negotiations said Bosnian leaders still had to resolve the organisation of the central bank, the design of coupons acceptable to all sides and for how long the coupons will be valid before the permanent currency is introduced.

Although the agreement was vague and left many questions unanswered, analysts in Sarajevo said that Bosnia's former enemies had inched towards forming the central bank as envisaged in the Dayton peace accord.

"The truth is, it is a step forward. We have a name of the new currency, we have a general endorsement of the fact that there will be one currency and one single bank," said a Western official who asked not to be named.
The presidency instructed the bank's board of governors to work out the details of the central bank law following the principles accepted on Tuesday.
The draft law must then be submitted to the presidency for consideration and adopted by the joint parliament.
The legistlation is among economic laws the international community is urging Bosnia to adopt if it wants to see foreign donors commit $1.4 billion for the country's reconstruction in 1997.

An international fund-raising conference had already been postponed twice since its original March date because the inter-ethnic government has failed to pass the required economic, tariff and foreign debt laws.

Bosnia also needs to clinch a deal with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) which wants to see a functioning central bank and budget laws adopted before the conference, likely to be held at the end of May in Brussels.
Analysts say international pressure over the postponed donors' conference helped produce an agreement in principle on the central bank.
The Bosnian Serbs, who only saw about two percent of foreign funds in 1996 out of $1.2 billion, are eager to catch up and revive their shattered economy.
The federation is already experiencing the benefits of reconstruction funds and wants more aid to get the economy moving.
But no one is sure when the central bank could come to life, officials said.
"Again, it comes down to the political will...We could have the draft of the law next week but it could also drag on forever," the official said.
